Phil Schaap

Phil Schaap was born in New York City on April 8, 1951. He grew up surrounded by jazz and its prominent players and began his career as a jazz DJ at WKCR in 1970. Phil has produced numerous recordings and is an important source of historical accuracy in jazz reissues. He has taught at Princeton and The New School and played an important role in Ken Burns’ documentary “Jazz.”
Phil was interviewed in Toronto, Canada on January 9, 2003 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Toronto for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m extremely pleased to have Phil Schaap with me here. I’m just going to call you a keeper of the jazz flame, and we can talk about the things you’ve done. You were just talking about, before the cameras were rolling, your teachers. And you mentioned Basie alumnus.

Yeah, well alumni actually, Jo Jones, who the only people who called him Papa Jo Jones when I met him were his children, and some of them were pretty young. A couple of them were not born yet. And he was significantly younger than I am now. I am 51 and he was 44. That’s significant. And Earle Warren, the leader of the reeds. I mean I don’t know whether it was coincidence or because of their camaraderie, which once I intersected with it facilitated more Basieites being involved with the nurturing of me as a child jazz enthusiast into someone who could perhaps hand off some of the information they gave me to subsequent generations of largely listeners, not performers. But from the trumpet section Buck Clayton and less Sweets Edison, because when I was very young he moved to California so he wasn’t a full timer but I knew Sweets well and he always was sweet to me. From the trombones, Dicky Wells and Eddie Durham and Benny Morton, I believe I met Benny last but perhaps heard him perform first. Then from the reeds Earle Warren, Buddy Tate. I met Lester Young a few times as a child but I didn’t really have a relationship with him. I’m still close to his family, his widow Mary, and children, Lester, and in fact particularly Lester Junior but Mary Young more than any, who I met when I was five, when they were in the neighborhood when she got her library card at the Jamaica Public Library and my mother was — I believe she was the chief librarian by then but that wasn’t such a big deal because I was sitting at her desk. There wasn’t child daycare yet and the lady came in for a library card and it was Mrs. Lester Young so my mother said to Mrs. Young, “Oh is your husband the saxophonist in the Basie band?” And she said yes. She said, “You seem to know about us.” And she said, “Well my little boy here knows more about it.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
And you were five?
Yeah. Maybe four. Probably five.
Okay. How come?
It’s a mid-fifties story.
Yeah. How come?
Because the music attracted me.
At age four?
And I had access to it.
Yeah. Because of your father?

Well why the music attracted me is probably something inside me that is not explainable. Why I had access to the music is probably a combination of my parents — let’s not forget Marjorie Schaap — and the proximity of the musicians who were making jazz to the Hollis Queens neighborhood where we moved on December 4, 1956, although we moved into my mother’s parent’s home. They had been in Hollis going back a long ways, I mean to colonial times. So we’re rooted, on my mother’s side, in an area which became the bedroom community of jazz in the earliest of my scholastic years, I mean elementary school, and so on a daily basis it seemed — it couldn’t possibly have been daily — but the people I had just found out about and become enthusiastic about instantaneously became neighbors. And that’s really the formula.
Oh that’s great. I’m just trying to picture a four and five year old pursuing Basie albums and that kind of thing. That’s a neat picture.

Well enthusiasm among children isn’t unusual, it’s that I was enthusiastic about jazz that you’re finding unusual. I probably was just as enthusiastic about sports at that time. I mean I could probably tell you as much about — at least statistically — about the major sports in those years as I could about jazz, as they were competing for my enthusiasms and jazz won somewhere in the middle of my adolescence. But every now and then a student of mine will be like from some city, let’s say Pittsburgh, and I’ll tell them everything about the Pittsburgh Pirates from roughly 1950 to 1965 maybe or 3, and then it will disappear and they won’t understand it you know. Why does it disappear? And the answer is because I’m teaching you jazz.
I see. Was the swing-based music of the Basie band something that your parents liked too?

Oh they were huge Basie enthusiasts, but that doesn’t mean they weren’t huge Benny Goodman enthusiasts, huge Fletcher Henderson enthusiasts. I would say that — I would say they didn’t have a Basie preference to my knowledge. I would say that my befriending more Basie alumni than say the Ellington people — remember the Ellington people, some of them still were in the band and therefore were not full time residents of © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

New York City, much less residents of the Hollis area. I knew Russell Procope well but he was largely gone. I eventually became quite close to Sam Woodyard, but this was later. I mean then it was the Basieites, and then through me having these unusual extra- parental associations I would say that my parents became more Basie core because when I emerged professionally that’s my first idea was a group of these Basie alumni playing the early Basie repertoire, to give some context to these gigs, and to play repertoire that Basie himself was largely no longer using.
For you what was it about the Basie sound that made it distinctive?

Well that it’s an orchestra that is able to incorporate, without everyone being a genius, the rhythmic revolution of the 1930s. But I don’t think I could have told you that in 1956. I mean in other words the suppleness of the beat that is elasticising and making more fluid the energy of swinging jazz rhythm.
Is that the rhythmic revolution?

That’s what I’m calling the rhythmic revolution of the thirties. There’s an innovation of genius. Roy Eldridge, Billie Holiday, Charlie Christian, Benny Carter, Benny Goodman, Teddy Wilson, Lester Young if I haven’t said him of course, and a few others. But the transference of it to others and the coherence of it as an ensemble display where the parts are combinable and examinable separately, I hear that merger in the Basie band first, other than an individual display. Billie Holiday displayed it on her lonesome, but the Basie band displayed it as an aggregation. And I think that that attracts me and clinches or adds musical substance to an emphasis that I place — because I knew, I mean Buddy Tate, of the inner core musicians who raised me and trained me, I mean I was fortunate in that none of the primaries died until I was nearly 30. I would say Russell Procope was the first close friend, extra family, extra father, to die and he died in January of ’81 and I was 29 in January of ’81, so I was pretty lucky in that regard considering how wide open I was to such setbacks and emotional challenges. And then with Buddy Tate’s death in February of I guess 2001, I lost the last one. It doesn’t mean that they are different than the musicians who I can’t say that about it’s just that they had hands on operation with me as a child and that I formed these bonds and now I’m kind of out on my own.
Right. How did you find them overall as people?

Well everybody’s different. And I can separate their identities. I believe there is a reason why Basie got these groups together. I believe they are individuals who created a connectable core to each other. I find the camaraderie of the Basie guys, it’s a moot point now except maybe in some larger sense, but there was a buddy system there that’s different from — but they’re all different. Eddie Durham for instance, probably was musically the most smart, best trained, clearly a genius. I would go so far to say that Durham must be the most underrated musical genius of the twentieth century. He’s the © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

first electric guitarist. He arranged “In the Mood” for Glenn Miller. He wrote the original Basie band book. He taught all these people. He wrote “Topsy,” he co-wrote the “One O’clock Jump” he really created the formula and he was very, very — not so much introverted as incredibly quiet and had no arguing desires in his make-up. I used to have these things I would mention to Eddie and he would tweak them for me. In a sense he would correct me, and then I would stick with my answer. And he would say, “Okay, Phil.” But of those, there’s only one left in which he was not right and I was not wrong. And I believe (a) that I am right, which would be the only time, which is a small point because there were thousands that he was right about, and (b) I’m not positive it’s provable but he still thinks — is it “Pigeon Walk” or is “Posin” it’s one or the other, it’s probably “Pigeon Walk,” by the Lunceford band, recorded in Los Angeles in the fall of ’37. He still thinks it’s he, the guitarist, and not Allen Norris on it. But he’s not on that record. And I believe that what Norris had done is taken the lessons and was able to, in this one instance, fake out the creator to think that it was himself. But staying on line with “Pigeon Walk,” when I first found this record, which you had to find, I believe on 78 it’s so long ago, or — I don’t think my father and mother had that in their collections. I had their libraries and my additional library. And I’ve got a lot of 78s when — remember the LPs demise and the CDs struck so LPs got real cheap. Well when they were clearing out the shelves of the 78s it was the same deal. I bought a lot of them by the pound. There was one record store, Triboro Records in Jamaica Queens that just had a little scale for 78s and they got rid of them man. They wouldn’t charge anything. And I actually, recognizing that the vinylite 78s of post World War II both weighed less and sounded better. Therefore one could get more records at this thing. I think that’s really where the start of my bebop interest is rooted. Because I suddenly had many more bebop 78s than my father or mother would have had. They would have few, and I suddenly had an out of balance percentage at this early juncture. Plus Russell intersected favorably with me at the age of four or possibly five, but I think it’s four because we were still living in Astoria, an area of Queens where we had an apartment before my grandfather retired and my father and mother bought the house and they went to Florida, we moved to Hollis. But Ross Russell was friendly with my parents and when he closed down the warehousing of the defunct Dial Record Company — I guess he had gone broke is what happened because he’s staying — you know there’s my bed and there’s a rollaway cot and it’s Ross Russell in our apartment, that doesn’t really sound like you have a nice luxurious little staying place here in a nice hotel. New York City has nice hotels but he’s staying and my parents I think took it as a holiday to go out and date a lot, with themselves I mean, because —
I see. Built in babysitter. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
Right. And he let me watch “The Tonight Show” which I think had just started, which had a lot of jazz on it then. He let me stay up as late as possible.
Yeah, they had a heck of a band.

So I have fond memories — this is the Steve Allen days if I’m not — I mean it’s either Steven Allen or pre-Steve Allen. I think it’s Steve Allen. And — definitely it was Steve Allen. And Ross Russell left behind a stack of yellow labeled Dial 78s for me which got mixed in with the Golden records and my Lester Young 78 and the ones that I — and so I have fond recollections. It’s sometimes hard for me on the air to point out that he’s guilty of many outright fictions when he clearly could have known better in writing his histories.
Yes. Well as a teenager, you had this —
Oh I didn’t finish the Durham thing, I’m sorry.
Oh okay, go ahead.

So Eddie Durham, so I got this “Pigeon Walk” which is what set us off on this course. I got it and I immediately noticed, hey, that’s the introduction to “Time Out,” which, and they’re both written by Eddie Durham. So I said well there’s a match. So I had met Eddie Durham so I ran with the record. You couldn’t make it on a cassette, although reel-to-reel tape existed I didn’t have access yet. I got one of those in ’61. So this is probably ’61 or earlier. And although this conversation happened again and again, and I said, “So Eddie, you know, it’s the same thing.” He said, “I got in a lot of trouble over that.” And then he said, “And you know and there’s even a third title, Phil, the original title, we didn’t call it ‘Time Out’ we called it ‘Count Nine.’” And I said “Count Nine?” So I listened to the introduction of “Time Out” and being not just inferior to Eddie Durham but just an inferior musician, I counted ten. So I said “Don’t you mean ‘Count Ten’ Eddie?” He said, “Okay Phil.” The point was he had had this earlier thing. But now I can’t even re-teach myself how to get it to ten. It’s count nine. He’s right, I’m wrong. This would be the first of the — I don’t know whether you’ve ever gotten Dan Morgenstern before this —
I have not.

But if you do, and you choose to bring this up it would be a small point in his life, “You Got Love” is a very obscure 1931 Benny Moten record which he purports, and he’s a very wise man, I mean this is no challenge to Dan Morgenstern’s magnificence and his majesty, but he says that that’s an uncredited Hot Lips Page vocal, the first Hot Lips Page vocal known. And you listen to the record and it makes a hell of a lot of sense. I played it for Eddie Durham and he states it’s Jimmy Rushing. It’s not Jimmy Rushing.
Yeah you can tell Jimmy Rushing, can’t you?
Oh, then you play the game and you make your own choice then you come back and we’ll talk. So he listens, and, “No, no, it’s Jimmy Rushing.” I said, “No it’s Lips.” “No © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

it’s Jimmy Rushing.” “It’s Lips.” And then he said, “Okay” and he never would debate it again with me because to get him to go three or four times was unusual. He must have either liked me or disliked me, because he’s going the extra yard. And it’s Jimmy Rushing. I’m wrong. No longer wrong. If Dan still says it’s Lips he’s — look out Dan — wrong. And Eddie Durham is once again — he completely backed off and didn’t mean anything, but he was right.
But how did you finally determine that?

I learned it. You know this is the punch line of studying for a lifetime. I know now. I’m not anywhere near Eddie Durham but I’m better than I was when I was eleven. And it’s Jimmy Rushing. That’s Jimmy Rushing singing “I Need That Love,” not Lips Page. Eddie Durham, as I said, there are like sixty of these little things and obviously I can’t give them all to your camera but of the sixty — so all sixty I thought I was right, all sixty I thought Eddie Durham was wrong. As it stands now Eddie Durham is right 59 times. I’m wrong 59 times and the one outstanding issue which I do pache Eddie Durham’s soul, I do believe this time Eddie is wrong, which is “The Pigeon Walk.” If it is “The Pigeon Walk,” I think it’s “Pigeon Walk” and the guitar solo by Allen Norris. It’s a Hollywood recording I believe from November 15 of ’37 and Eddie Durham couldn’t have been there.
I see. Well I hope you get to keep that one.
I hope I lose it.
That means you’re still learning.

It does. It also means Eddie Durham is as great as I say he is, and he is. So it was Eddie Durham in the trombones and Benny Morton and Dicky Wills. I wasn’t too close with Vic. Vic was kind of shy I betcha. And to get children into his inner circle, he liked to talk to musicians and adults. And so, and I had such a friendship with Dicky Wells that took me all around. Dicky is my meal ticket, my ace — and he was so brilliant. Dicky Wells was wise too but Eddie Durham was the genius and wrote all that stuff. And then Earle Warren led the reeds. And he was the one I was closest to, because he was the leader and he was a teacher and he was a father. He did something that — I don’t know how much teaching you do but he did something with young people that I’m still trying to do, much less do as well. He’s the only one I’ve ever seen do this. I talk with Wynton Marsalis a lot about this because he doesn’t know — he knows Earle Warren but didn’t realize that if he led the reeds in that band he must be great. And I was asleep on him, so tell me about him. You know so like that’s really my function. I hung out with Earle Warren for 35 years and you get to hear about it because you can. That’s the formula. That’s why this is such a great thing that’s going on. If any of this is great and if I can convey it well or suitably. But Earle Warren’s most amazing talent to me — independent © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

of his musical greatness — was that you know adolescents are rebellious. They’re not necessarily political or socially oriented. I mean I think the youth movement concept is a little bit overrated. It happened in my generation in America and perhaps even internationally but it doesn’t always happen. But rebelliousness and fighting off the direction and wisdom, pontifications of the elder generation, that battle ground has been around, according to Aristotle, at least 3000 years, and Earle Warren is the only person who when it’s a cold line in the dirt, you’re on that side and I’m on this side, you’re the young person and Earle Warren, and he could say “listen I understand where you’re coming from, let me explain this to you.” And do it. And explain it so that everything calms down and that he could explain to the student or youngster why they were wrong, get them to accept it, to understand that it wasn’t just some browbeating coming down from on high, and to adapt it in some way, to synthesize it. And I’ve never seen anyone do it as well as Earle Warren did it. Absolutely outstanding ability to explain a complete difference of opinion over a generation gap and win — it’s not a competition, he knew that — to explain it. And to find common ground and good action from both sides.
Quite a talent.

I’ve never found it again. I’d like to have it. And let’s not leave out Jo Jones, the original, the babysitter, you know I was going to Jo Jones’ apartment learning jazz lessons from Jo Jones, it’s a tough struggle, but I knew him and he was great.
What kinds of things did he teach you?

How to listen to records so you didn’t say something stupid. That’s an important lesson. Him and Al Hibbler. Say, “Monk, who do you think’s playing alto on this record?” And you’d say, “Well I don’t know.” “You can’t tell, Monk?” “No I can’t.” “Well tell you what. Here’s the record. Listen to it for a week. Come back next Saturday morning. But if you can’t tell me next Saturday morning give me back the record and don’t come here no more.” Now that’s a tough teaching — their method. I hope I’m not that mean. But they weren’t mean to me.
I see. Were your parents thrilled that you were getting this?
Yes. No. My mother was eventually thrilled. She was fighting the sports and music thing. I mean her idea was — I wanted to learn an instrument and it was violin or nothing so I said nothing.
She said violin or nothing.

Yeah. She may not — I may be making her out to be more shrewish, she was a zany Bohemian jazz lover. But she didn’t want — I guess she wanted the best for me and she had to figure out what the best was at the time. So I got involved in singing with my boy soprano in the major music program of the New York City public school system which was an excellent program in those days. Always yearning to be in the instrumental © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

program and the enriched program — they call it SPE — or they called it I gather, I have no idea whether it still exists in the New York City public school system. But SPE is a special program for good, gifted students. But the E meant there’d be some music component. Enriched is what it stood for. And you either went into the band or you went into the chorus. And I wanted that band bad. But I’d been singing on an enriched music program with this boy soprano fourth, fifth and sixth grade because I had done okay on the recorder class, they give you some recorder lessons and I did okay, so and then I passed some listening test which probably I shouldn’t have passed because I’m not that good. And they wouldn’t let me take an instrument. So I started studying trumpet on the side on my own in adolescence. But my mother, my grandfather, her father, was an excellent musician, an organist, a church organist, but he was a lawyer. And my father’s father was a lawyer. And lawyer — they discovered this memory, you know when I was two I could do the presidents, forward and backward, with their dates. I still can do it but I do it slower than I did in 1953. And it’s not just because there are more presidents since Truman, it’s that some of them are more forgettable than Truman. And you know so she wanted that. And I loved those Brooklyn Dodgers and — “You don’t take my son to baseball games” she really didn’t want me to go to the sports things. And fortunately for me if thwarting that is important, was that my illustrious cousin, you know, hit big time sports right then and started like free ticket city. That would be Dick Schaap. He died just slightly more than a year ago. And he went with Newsweek and Sport Magazine right around the time I entered elementary school and the next, until he was city editor of the Herald Tribune which would be like ’63 or ‘4, it was sports heaven in a Schaap house, any Schaap household. I mean what does Billy Crystal say? They’re pretty tight, Billy Crystal and my late cousin were very tight, he says, “What is the first thing you think of when you think of Dick Schaap?” “Tickets.” And boy he wasn’t in the family. And it’s funny, you know during that time I knew Billy Crystal’s father. He stunned — I mean Billy Crystal is close friends of this area of our family, the Schaap family, they are tight. But I knew Jack Crystal and Bernhardt Crystal, Jack’s brother, who still lives. And I’ve only met Billy Crystal and spoken with him largely about his father. And I actually have something that Billy Crystal wants from me. I have — Jack Crystal used to let me into the Central Plaza for cheap. I don’t think he let me in for free, but he let me in for cheap. And Billy Crystal said, “Did you save the ticket stubs?” And my mother was half pack rat and half insane throw outer. So the autograph collection and the programs, my Scotty LaFaro autograph and all the others, it’s gone. But one ticket stub, I must have put it in the wrong place, from the Central Plaza. And he wants the Central Plaza ticket stub. I always said this Dixieland club, very close to where the Filmore was a few years later that Jack Crystal, after he — he didn’t really break with Milt Gabler, after all they were © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

brother-in-laws — but he got out of the Commodore Music Shop. And he was nice to me. Jack Crystal was nice to me. And Billy Crystal liked that, and Dick Schaap liked that because it was so odd, and Bernhardt, he can’t believe, I’m the only guy he meets who doesn’t know his famous nephew and does know his late brother.
Oh really. But your father liked the fact that you had all these associations with these musicians.

Yeah my mother did too. I mean we went to the events. But the person who I’m leaving out from a family thing is that so my father and mother took me to these things, and I went out and then the musicians took me to some of these things. But my cousin Bill, Bill Schaap, Dick’s younger brother, he stepped into the breech and started, I piggy backed on his enthusiasms and goodness. I mean he’s a good guy. His wife stopped answering the telephone because I took him out of the house and I guess she didn’t like jazz. He took me to see everything. We even booed Dylan at Gerde’s Folk City, which wasn’t called Gerde’s yet, it was just Folk City. I think it was before they took over Tony Pastor’s joint, before they moved. And the only reason why I know it was Dylan who we booed is because he became famous so quickly after. Because they would have the new folk singer who wanted to be the next Pete Seeger I guess or Dylan would probably say Woody Guthrie. And they would be the emcee but they would do a few songs at the start of the show. And I really wasn’t into — there was this Hootenanny craze.
Yes, sure.
So we’re in the same tribe, huh Monk, yeah, yeah, yeah? You seem to know as much about the fifties and sixties.
Yeah, we’re very close.

But it was cool with me but it wasn’t cool. And so if you wanted to go to Folk City to see a blues act, because they had blues acts, like Sonny Terry, who was my neighbor. I used to hit home runs, whiffle ball into his yard. I think he lived at the corner of Keno and Pompey in Hollis. And we didn’t want to hear this unknown folk singer do his thing, so you booed him to make sure he didn’t do an encore or anything.
Really.
Oh yeah. It didn’t matter whether it was Dylan or not. Whoever it was you booed.
Oh. Okay.

Let’s say this was the bill. You know, I’m not saying this was the bill, you have Joan Baez, Pete Seeger, Peter, Paul & Mary, Benny Goodman and an unknown folk singer. And so if I went to that, I went to hear Benny Goodman. Even though Peter, Paul & Mary and Joan Baez and all these others are famous people, I’ll tolerate them because they’re famous, I want to hear what they have to do, but I’m going to be sitting on my hands for three hours waiting for the Benny Goodman or whatever, Sonny Terry and Brownie © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

McGee which I went to see many times. That’s what I want to see. So I’m not going to encourage an encore. I’m trying to get rid of this thing. But because he became famous so fast I remembered it was him.
Sure. Well he had a pretty distinctive sound at the time too.

Yeah but that wasn’t it, it was just he was the guy and you booed him. I booed others whose names I don’t know. I know him because he became famous. Every time I went to Folk City it was to see the blues act. Never once to see the folk act. Not once. It doesn’t make them bad, it doesn’t hopefully make me bad. But I went to see the blues act. And so the new hootenanny wannabe who was the emcee got short shrift from me, and my cousin Bill, and at one time it was Dylan.
Okay. Well when you got to be 17, 18 thinking what kind of outlet is there for this passion I have—

Yeah. I thought about it a lot, surprisingly a lot. I scoped out what I wanted to do pretty quickly and stuck to it very seriously. I mean for a minute there I wanted to be a trumpet player. I got a trumpet and I practiced too much, as my neighbors I’m sure could tell you, and I got a little bit of facility in the upper register, but I played stupid. And I was smart enough to know I was playing stupid. When I played with rock & roll bands, you know, I just recently ran into this guy, he actually had a minor career in big time rock & roll, Lou Erlanger. I think he goes as Lou X. Erlanger. He was with Mink Deville and a couple of other things. But they had a band called the Stingrays. And I helped them. Because they were good. And they thought I was good. And they were wrong. And I’m still wondering what on earth — and I recently met Lou again for a jazz reason I’m pleased to say and you know he still remembers that he dug me. Because I swung better than they did, no offense, Lou and his band, the Stingrays. And they were encouraging me. But I was impressed at their facility on their instruments and their intonation. They were better on electric guitar than I was on trumpet, and they played in tune. I had an upper register on trumpet but I had a shrill tone and I got excited and I played woefully out of tune, sharp largely, which I can hear. Good enough to hear it, not good enough to stop. So I stopped playing. And the other reason why was because of my sound career. I made a few gigs at a place called the McGill House in Jamaica, Queens. This was — I mean from my point of view I mean I was doing nothing. We played, a trombone player, a tenor player and me, we’d play a chord behind some singer trying to be the next Diana Ross. She wasn’t that famous yet, there was just the Supremes. Or something like that. And that was the gig. And then downstairs — it was really actually a very well run operation. Downstairs they had like, it was more like Gerde’s Folk City. It wasn’t so much the hootenanny thing but the protest folk music thing which is a little more interesting to me, and then with like apple cider and donuts and people you could talk to © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

and I’m sure I was attracted to a couple of young females who I went to high school with down there. But I was playing with the rhythm & blues, or soul as it was starting to be called, upstairs. And the sound was good. And I used to talk to the sound guy. And then I’d go hear Roy Eldridge, that was say a Saturday night dance on Sunday I’d say, “Roy, you know the sound isn’t too good.” He said “I’m hip, tell me about it, please believe me I need help.” And gradually I became an audio guy. And this really, I think, triggered the idea of helping the musicians who deserve to be helped rather than becoming an undeserving musician. And that transition occurs over the late 60s and basically my Columbia college years. And I’m out of the trumpet business. Well I played Milestones at the West End on March 11, 1974 with Paul Quinichette and Matthew Gee, and Sam Woodyard. And I was playing Frank Williams’ horn so he wasn’t playing. I don’t know who was on piano. It might have been Frank Williams, he had good piano playing. Or that might have been it. There may have been no chordal root. But we were playing a modal piece so that makes sense. There was no chordal root. And then Gee and Quinichette, who pache, their souls were drunks, they laid out on the bridge you know, and I think there’s an E above the staff you’ve got to hit twice in the bridge [humms], there was just me out in the open, me and Woodyard. And I said I’ll never do that again in life. And I haven’t. I did play my notes right then, and so I said I’m batting a thousand, time to retire.
Right. Well you got into the radio through Columbia University.

Absolutely. And through my sound career. Oh yeah. Jon Hendricks went crazy over that this morning here at the IAJE so I now realize that he wants me to put it down on paper, and to mail it to him. But you’re getting a thing. It’s cause there’s no way you’re going to be able to reprise that rhythm section concept with no understanding. So this is — and this is a little bit too harsh. I’m cutting things — it’s too concise, too pat, doesn’t leave enough room for the obvious exceptions that prove numerous other rules. This is the story. So you’ve got four guys. You’ve got piano, bass, guitar — acoustic guitar — and drums. Okay the bass. The bass player is in charge of four. Meaning he’s in charge of four four. The four four feel, that’s the bass player’s job. It’s got to be four four. The guitar player is in charge — it’s not in two four, but two four is always being played inside the four four. That’s the guitar player’s gig. The guitar player is in charge of two four, even though he’s playing in four four as well. It can’t be too bad, it has to be subtle, it has to be there.
